passage: Looking back at Class Ten, I think I was tired for a whole year. My day was an hour on the school bus, a classroom with fifty-five of us, then tuition until eight, then homework. I hardly saw the sky except through a bus window. At night I scrolled through pictures of other people's marks and holidays and felt small. Payal, who sat two benches away, was the only one who noticed. One day Payal said, "You look like you haven't laughed in ages." I said I was fine. Then I cried. Payal didn't try to fix anything, just started walking with me to the small park behind school for fifteen minutes every afternoon. It doesn't sound like much, but I began to feel like a person again. Vasudha

qa.q: How many students were in Vasudha's classroom?
qa.a: There were fifty-five of them in the classroom.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when scrolling through other people's marks and holidays?
qa.a: Vasudha felt small, tired and lonely, comparing the crowded days with everyone else's pictures.

qa.q: Which choice by Payal helped Vasudha begin to feel better?
qa.a: Payal noticed and asked, did not try to fix anything, and started walking with Vasudha to the small park behind school for fifteen minutes every afternoon.

qa.q: What might Payal have been thinking when noticing that Vasudha had not laughed in ages?
qa.a: Payal was probably concerned and caring, and noticed something the others missed.

grounding: A city teenager faces a crowded school, tuition, traffic and comparison with little open space, and loneliness eases when a friend notices and makes room to breathe.

passage: Counsellor's note, Class 10. Jagdish, 15, came to see me after his teacher said he seemed distracted. He described a day: school from seven, tuition until nine, a two-hour journey in traffic, and a phone full of classmates' marks and holidays. He said, "Everyone seems ahead. And I haven't spoken to anyone properly in weeks." He has stopped playing football. I did not tell him to work less or more. We listed which activities he chose and which he was only following. I asked if he would like me to speak with his parents, and he said yes. On Thursday we met them, and they agreed to drop one tuition slot for football on Saturday mornings. I will see Jagdish again in two weeks. Sharmila, school counsellor

qa.q: How long is Jagdish's journey in traffic?
qa.a: Jagdish's journey in traffic takes two hours.

qa.q: What is Jagdish feeling when he says everyone seems ahead?
qa.a: Jagdish feels behind and lonely, comparing himself with others and having had no real conversation with anyone in weeks.

qa.q: Which choice by Jagdish opened the way to a change?
qa.a: Jagdish said yes when asked if the counsellor could speak with his parents, so they could agree to drop a tuition slot for football.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's parents have seen the situation before the meeting?
qa.a: Possibly unaware of how heavy his day felt. Once they heard it, they agreed to drop one tuition slot, which shows they cared.

grounding: A city teenager faces crowded days, tuition, traffic and comparison with little open space, and a counsellor and parents make room for balance.

passage:
In Hong Kong, Yosef, fifteen, woke at six, rode a packed bus for fifty minutes, sat through seven hours of classes, then went straight to maths tuition until eight. On the bus home, he scrolled through photos of classmates skiing, winning prizes, laughing on rooftops. He felt tired and somehow behind.
His friend Wei sat next to him. "You haven't laughed all week."
"There's no time to laugh."
Wei thought. "Come to the hill trail with me on Saturday morning. Before tuition. One hour."
Yosef almost said no. But on Saturday they climbed the trail above the city. The air was cool. They could see the whole harbour, tiny and quiet.
Yosef realised he hadn't looked at his phone for an hour. He felt lighter, for the first time in weeks.
"Same time next week?" Wei asked. Yosef nodded.

qa.q: How long was Yosef's bus ride?
qa.a: Yosef rode a packed bus for fifty minutes.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling as he scrolled through classmates' photos?
qa.a: He felt tired and somehow behind, comparing his busy, joyless week to their highlights.

qa.q: What small step helped balance Yosef's week?
qa.a: A one-hour walk on the hill trail with Wei, away from his phone, gave him open space and a friend, which made him feel lighter.

qa.q: How might Wei feel about Yosef's week?
qa.a: Wei seems concerned and caring, noticing that Yosef hasn't laughed and wanting to help.

grounding: A city teenager outside India faces packed days, tuition and online comparison, and a weekly walk with a friend begins to ease stress and loneliness.

passage:
At the coaching centre in Kota, Shalini, sixteen, had a desk, a hostel bed, and a timetable pinned to the wall: school, coaching, self-study, sleep. Her weekly test rank was posted on a board every Monday. This week she'd slipped from 42 to 88.
Online, everyone seemed to be topping and celebrating.
Chandrika, from the next room, sat down with two cups of tea. "You've skipped dinner three days."
Shalini's voice cracked. "I came here for this. My parents took so much trouble. And I just feel alone."
Chandrika didn't give advice. She said, "Me too. Let's walk on the terrace every night after study. Just us, no phones."
Later that night, Shalini called her mother and told her the truth about the rank and the loneliness. Her mother said, "Come home for a weekend. We'll talk. Rank isn't everything." The next morning Shalini also booked a slot with the centre's counsellor.

qa.q: What was Shalini's rank this week?
qa.a: She'd slipped from 42 to 88.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when her voice cracked?
qa.a: Shalini felt lonely, pressured and guilty about her parents' effort, overwhelmed by the rank and comparison.

qa.q: Which steps helped balance Shalini's stress?
qa.a: A nightly phone-free walk with Chandrika, an honest call to her mother the same night, and booking the counsellor gave her connection and support.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's life at the centre feel?
qa.a: Chandrika seems to feel the same loneliness, which is why she says "Me too" and suggests walking together.

grounding: A teenager in a crowded city coaching centre faces rank pressure, comparison and loneliness, and friendship, family and a counsellor help balance it.

passage:
Dear Saurabh,
You asked what city life is like. You said you're jealous because we have malls and fast internet and the metro.
It's true, there's lots to do. But here's my day: school till two, tuition till six, homework till ten. The traffic takes an hour each way. Our building has no garden, and the only park nearby has "No Playing" signs.
Everyone at school posts photos looking perfect. I compare myself all the time. Sometimes I feel lonely even in a crowded class.
Last month I visited your village. Remember how we lay on the haystack and talked till midnight? I haven't felt that calm in a year.
Mumma says I need a balance, so now I go to a Saturday dance class and I don't open my phone after nine. It helps a bit.
Write back and tell me about the fields.
Sabina

qa.q: How long does the traffic take each way?
qa.a: The traffic takes an hour each way.

qa.q: How does Sabina feel about city life?
qa.a: Sabina feels stressed and sometimes lonely even in a crowded class, and misses the calm of the village.

qa.q: What small steps is Sabina taking for balance?
qa.a: Sabina goes to a Saturday dance class and doesn't open the phone after nine, which helps a bit.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see city life after reading the letter?
qa.a: Saurabh may realise that the malls and metro come with pressure and loneliness, and see village life a little differently.

grounding: A city teenager writes about crowded days, tuition and comparison, admitting the loneliness behind the gains and seeking balance.

passage: Six-fifteen alarm, six-fifty bus, and the bus takes forty minutes in Gurugram traffic if we're lucky. That's my morning. I'm Parul, Class 11, and people tell me I'm lucky to live in a city with everything, and I am: three libraries, a coding club, the best tuition teachers. But after school it's tuition till eight, then homework, then I scroll and see everyone's trips and toppers' lists and feel I'm already behind at sixteen. There's no ground near our society, just a parking lot. Last month my friend Vaibhav made me walk with him around the lot after dinner, twenty minutes, no phones. It sounds so silly. But it's the only part of my day nobody grades. I sleep better on the days we walk.

qa.q: Where do Parul and Vaibhav walk after dinner?
qa.a: They walk around the parking lot after dinner.

qa.q: What does Parul feel when scrolling after homework?
qa.a: Parul feels anxious and behind, comparing a crowded day with everyone's trips and toppers' lists.

qa.q: What small balance in Parul's day seems to help, and why?
qa.a: The twenty-minute walk with no phones gives a space nobody grades, easing the stress and helping sleep.

qa.q: Why might Vaibhav have insisted on the walks?
qa.a: Vaibhav probably noticed Parul looking stressed or lonely and cared enough to start a small, calm routine they could share.

grounding: It illustrates a city teenager with real gains in choice and speed but crowded days, tuition and online comparison, and a small balance that eases stress.
